title: Elevator System
context: A concurrency-flavoured design that is really about strategy: 'which car serves which request' is a policy, and policies should be pluggable. Watch for designs where the Elevator class also implements the scheduling algorithm.
statement:
Design the low-level structure for a bank of elevators in a building.

The building has N floors and M elevator cars. Passengers press an up/down call button on a floor; inside a car they press a destination floor button. A controller decides which car serves which call. Each car moves between floors, opens/closes doors, and must not accept new requests while its doors are open or while moving in a direction that cannot serve the request.

The default dispatch policy is 'nearest suitable car', but the building owner may later switch to zoning (cars dedicated to floor ranges) or peak-hour scheduling.

Safety-relevant behaviour: doors must close before the car moves; a car must not exceed its weight limit; emergency stop brings all cars to the nearest floor.

Your design should make the dispatch policy replaceable and keep the car's own mechanics separate from the building-wide decision logic.

requirements.text: Floor calls (up/down) and in-car destination requests are distinct request types and both must be modelled.
A controller/scheduler decides which car serves which request; the policy is replaceable (nearest car, zoning, peak-hour).
Each car models its own mechanics: current floor, direction, door state, and movement.
Safety invariants: doors closed before moving, weight limit respected, emergency stop handled.
A car only accepts requests it can serve given its direction and door state (no impossible assignments).
The building owns the fleet: cars are registered, and the system works for any N floors / M cars.

thinkingHints: Who runs the loop — does the controller push commands to cars, or do cars pull their next stop?
Where does the weight-limit check live?
Is 'nearest suitable car' a method on the controller, or a strategy object? Why?
